hints: Focus on what Period 3 oxides and chlorides actually do in cold water, dissolving, staying as solid, or hydrolysing to make a new solid.
List the four water-insoluble cases first: sparingly soluble MgO, unreactive $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ and $\text{SiO}_2$, plus $\text{SiCl}_4$ which hydrolyses to fresh $\text{SiO}_2$.
With excess $\text{NaOH}$, remember $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ stays white but amphoteric aluminium dissolves, and fresh gelatinous silica dissolves much more easily than bulk sand.
walkthrough:
**Sort the oxides in water**

Think like this, does it dissolve, react to dissolve, or just sit there as a white powder?

$$\text{Na}_2\text{O} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{NaOH (aq, colourless, no solid)}$$

**Spot the insoluble oxides**

$\text{MgO}$ forms sparingly soluble white $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$, so most of 1.0 g stays solid. $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ and $\text{SiO}_2$ are giant structures and do not react with cold water, so they remain as white solids.

That is 3 solids so far from oxides.

**Sort the chlorides in water**

$\text{NaCl}$ and $\text{MgCl}_2$ are ionic and simply dissolve to colourless solutions. $\text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$ dissolves to acidic $\text{[Al(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{3+}$ solution with no precipitate.

$$\text{SiCl}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{SiO}_2\text{(s, white)} + 4\text{HCl(aq)}$$

**Count Q**

White solids after water are $\text{MgO}$ beaker, $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ beaker, $\text{SiO}_2$ beaker, and $\text{SiCl}_4$ beaker. So Q = 4.

**Add excess NaOH, watch for new precipitates and dissolving**

$\text{MgCl}_2$ beaker now gives white $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$, which is basic only and will NOT dissolve in excess $\text{NaOH}$:
$$\text{Mg}^{2+} + 2\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{Mg(OH)}_2\text{(s, white)}$$
$\text{MgO}$ beaker already contains $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ and it also stays solid.

**Use amphoteric behaviour and fresh vs bulk solid idea to get R**

Bulk $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ and bulk $\text{SiO}_2$ are very unreactive in cold dilute $\text{NaOH}$ in a beaker, so they stay as white solids. Fresh $\text{SiO}_2$ from $\text{SiCl}_4$ is finely divided and dissolves to silicate, and aluminium from $\text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$ first precipitates then redissolves:
$$\text{Al(OH)}_3 + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{[Al(OH)}_4\text{]}^-\text{(aq, colourless)}$$
So we lose the $\text{SiCl}_4$ solid but gain the $\text{MgCl}_2$ solid. Final white solids are $\text{MgO}$, $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$, $\text{SiO}_2$, $\text{MgCl}_2$ beakers. So R = 4.

options.A: Q = 3 misses one white solid, usually the fresh $\text{SiO}_2$ from $\text{SiCl}_4$ hydrolysis. R = 2 also misses that bulk $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ and $\text{SiO}_2$ stay undissolved in cold dilute $\text{NaOH}$ and that $\text{MgCl}_2$ forms $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$.
options.B: Q = 3 is too low because $\text{MgO}$, $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$, $\text{SiO}_2$ and hydrolysed $\text{SiCl}_4$ all give white solid. R = 3 then undercounts the $\text{MgCl}_2$ precipitate plus the three remaining bulk solids.
options.C: Q = 4 is correct, but R = 3 is wrong. Students often think $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ from $\text{MgCl}_2$ dissolves like $\text{Al(OH)}_3$, or think bulk $\text{SiO}_2$ or $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ dissolves completely in cold $\text{NaOH}$. Only amphoteric aluminium redissolves, magnesium does not.
options.D: Q = 4 from $\text{MgO}$, $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$, $\text{SiO}_2$ and $\text{SiCl}_4$ (as fresh $\text{SiO}_2$). After excess $\text{NaOH}$, $\text{MgO}$ stays as $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$, bulk $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ and bulk $\text{SiO}_2$ stay, $\text{MgCl}_2$ forms new $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$, while $\text{SiCl}_4$ solid dissolves and $\text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$ ends as soluble aluminate. So R = 4.
